video_title: The Canada-US Trade War: A Bridge Too Far? w/ Jesse Huebsch
gist: Process engineer Jesse Huebsch and host Chris Keefer argue the Canada-US trade war is a structural 'ratchet' (each Republican term adds barriers Democrats never fully reverse) rather than a temporary Trump aberration, and map Canada's real chokepoints -- the Gordie Howe Bridge financing dispute, the Line 5 pipeline, F-35 vs. Gripen parts control, and Westinghouse's AP-1000 -- while arguing US steel/aluminum tariffs are purely inflationary but auto tariffs could actually reshore production because US assembly plants already have spare capacity.

themes.theme: The Ratchet Theory of US Trade Policy

insights.claim: Trade barriers between the US and Canada are likely to ratchet upward across political cycles because America-first Republican administrations add new trade restrictions while subsequent Democratic administrations (as under Biden after Trump's first term) neither escalate further nor roll back what was already imposed, producing a one-way 'staircase' of protectionism rather than a return to the pre-Trump baseline.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: Investors should assume any tariffs or trade restrictions imposed during a Republican term become the new permanent floor, not a temporary shock that reverts when Democrats retake office.
insights.quote: We end out with a bit of a staircase and that's probably the optimistic scenario.

insights.claim: The odds of Democrats retaking and then holding the US presidency for more than eight years after 2028 should be viewed with concern because the economic damage from the current tariff regime is likely to come home to roost during the next election cycle, which could instead entrench an America-first Republican faction for a second consecutive term.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: Canadian and international investors planning multi-year capital projects to reduce US dependency should not assume a 2028 Democratic win resets trade policy back to pre-2025 conditions.

insights.claim: Canada should time major infrastructure investments meant to break critical US dependencies (e.g., an all-Canadian oil pipeline) to be completed by 2032-2033, on the assumption that a future America-first Republican administration -- not necessarily this one -- is the real risk window planners need to de-risk against.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: Capital allocators evaluating Canadian nation-building/infrastructure projects (pipelines, rail, ports) should model a ~2032 completion target as the relevant strategic deadline, not near-term economics alone.

insights.claim: There is no single rationale behind the Trump administration's Canada policy; it results from multiple competing factions simultaneously pursuing an escalated 'friend-shoring' response to the China shock (now amplified into 'bring everything home'), a desire to treat Canada as a resource colony for critical minerals, a personal ambition to be remembered as the president who expanded US territory (fed by Mercator-projection maps making Canada/Greenland look large), and admiration for the unconstrained freedom of action enjoyed by autocratic leaders.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: Investors trying to predict US trade policy should stop searching for one coherent objective and instead track which internal faction currently has leverage, since policy can whipsaw between rationales.
insights.quote: Each of those factions has their own reasons and they are can be you know mutually contradictory reasons and they can bubble up to the surface at times. So all of the reasons can be somewhat true.

insights.claim: Bombardier, a Canadian aerospace manufacturer, was tariffed hard on its C Series commercial jet and ended up divesting it to Airbus, leaving Bombardier focused on private business jets -- illustrated by the guest and host as a concrete precedent for the Trump administration's 'build it here or lose the market' pressure on Canadian manufacturers.
insights.speaker: Chris Keefer
insights.so_what: Canadian manufacturers with a single-country export concentration to the US remain exposed to tariff actions that can force divestiture of entire product lines, as already happened with Bombardier's C Series.

insights.claim: A bilateral trade deficit with one specific partner is not inherently meaningful -- only a country's aggregate trade balance with the rest of the world matters -- illustrated by the analogy that running a personal trade deficit with Costco is not a problem as long as one's overall trade position (with an employer) balances out.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: Investors should discount political rhetoric about the Canada-US bilateral goods deficit as a standalone red flag; the relevant metric is the US's aggregate trade position, not any single partner relationship.
insights.quote: I have a massive trade deficit with Costco. They have never uh you know they have never paid me directly a penny, but I've spent thousands of dollars there.

insights.claim: The US goods-trade deficit with Canada is driven almost entirely by Canada selling crude oil, a raw material the US refines into higher-value products and then resells domestically or exports -- meaning the 'deficit' actually reflects the US capturing value-add on Canadian raw inputs rather than an unfair imbalance.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: The oil-driven nature of the deficit undercuts the political case for broad Canada tariffs and suggests targeted energy-sector friction is more likely than a resolution addressing 'the deficit' as a whole.

insights.claim: When services are included (e.g., revenue Google and Microsoft earn in Canada, plus other professional services), the US runs a services trade surplus with Canada that largely offsets the oil-driven goods deficit, so on a total basis the US-Canada trade relationship is close to balanced.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: Framing US-Canada trade purely around the goods deficit overstates any imbalance; a full accounting including services shows minimal net imbalance, weakening the tariff justification.

insights.claim: By definition, a country that runs a sustained capital account surplus (pulling in foreign investment, as the US does) must run a matching trade deficit, since currency flows require that inflow of investment capital to be offset by an outflow of dollars via imports.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: The US trade deficit is a structural counterpart of its role as the destination for global investment capital, not simply evidence of unfair foreign trade practices -- a point relevant to any 'fix the deficit' policy thesis.

insights.claim: Canada's average tariff on US goods entering Canada was roughly 1% or a fraction of 1% before the trade war, meaning claims that Canadian protectionism justified reciprocal US tariffs have little empirical support outside a small number of mutually-agreed carve-outs like dairy supply management (matched on the US side by sugar and tobacco quotas).
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: Investors assessing the legitimacy of US tariff justifications against Canada should note the pre-existing Canadian tariff wall was negligible, implying the current dispute is driven by other political motives rather than correcting real trade barriers.

themes.theme: Why Steel/Aluminum Tariffs Fail but Auto Tariffs Could Work

insights.claim: US tariffs on aluminum will not induce new domestic primary aluminum smelting capacity because aluminum production is essentially 'liquefied electricity,' and any prospective US smelter investor must compete for power against AI data-center operators (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) who imply a marginal value of power around $1,000/MWh, while a smelter needs electricity priced in the tens of dollars per MWh to be viable.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: Tariff-driven reshoring theses for energy-intensive metals (aluminum, and by extension other electricity-heavy manufacturing) are undermined by AI data-center demand bidding up power prices well beyond what smelters can pay -- a structural headwind independent of policy.
insights.quote: aluminum being essentially liqufied electricity... you are competing against open AI, Anthropic, Google etc. to buy every scrap of electricity you can get their hands on and they have an implicit marginal value to power of about $1,000 a megawatt hour and you need to be able to get it in the tens.

insights.claim: Only about 16% of the aluminum used in the United States is domestically produced primary aluminum, so aluminum tariffs mainly let existing US and importing producers raise prices across the board (a windfall for a small domestic base) rather than build meaningful new supply, making the policy net inflationary.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: Aluminum-consuming industries in the US should expect sustained higher input costs from these tariffs with little offsetting increase in secure domestic supply, a durable cost/inflation input for downstream manufacturers.
insights.quote: I think it's 16% of ... primary aluminum in the US is domestic.

insights.claim: Auto tariffs on Canada are more likely to achieve their reshoring goal than metals tariffs because the US automotive industry already has significant spare assembly capacity, so simply forcing Canadian-based competitors to shut down redirects existing demand to already-built US plants without requiring new capital investment -- unlike aluminum, where new capacity requires decades-long investment decisions.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: Policy targeting industries with existing spare capacity (autos) is structurally more effective at near-term reshoring than policy targeting capital-intensive commodity production (aluminum/steel), a distinction investors should apply when judging which tariffs will 'bite.'

insights.claim: Collapsing Canadian auto production risks breaking the deeply cross-integrated North American auto parts supply chain (parts makers are not siloed by brand or country), which could create sudden critical-component shortages that halt production broadly, so any 'clean win' from auto tariffs carries significant supply-chain fragility risk.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: Auto sector investors should price in supply-chain disruption risk from tariff-driven consolidation, not just the headline reshoring narrative.

insights.claim: A full domestic EV supply chain is considered a national-security priority by at least one Trump administration faction not because of EVs themselves, but because EV components -- batteries, power electronics, injection-molded parts, basic chips/image-recognition processors, and processed critical minerals -- are essentially the same components required for mass drone production, which the Ukraine and Iran conflicts have shown to be central to modern medium-intensity warfare.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: Defense and industrial-policy investors should read US EV/battery reshoring pushes as a drone-manufacturing-capacity strategy, which changes the risk calculus for battery/EV-component supply chains being treated as strategic assets subject to export or ownership restrictions.
insights.quote: A seat in a car looks a lot like a drone... it's a similar size, a similar number of components, similar types... of components.

insights.claim: Canada fully financed the Gordie Howe Bridge (Detroit-Windsor), including construction on the US side using US materials, and offered to split toll revenue evenly with Michigan only after Canada's loan was repaid; at the last minute the Trump administration used its control over customs-plaza approval to threaten indefinite delay of the bridge's opening in order to extract a renegotiated revenue-sharing deal before the loan was paid off.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: This precedent shows the US administration is willing to use any available administrative lever to extract concessions even against a deal that was already more than fair to the US side, which should raise the risk premium Canadian planners assign to any future joint US-Canada infrastructure or contractual arrangement.

insights.claim: The Gordie Howe Bridge episode demonstrates that the Trump administration will pull any leverage lever available to it regardless of long-term negative consequences, if it provides short-term advantage -- reframing Canada's infrastructure planning around eliminating 'critical vulnerabilities' (disproportionate short-term leverage points) rather than general economic efficiency.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: Any Canada-US joint infrastructure, defense, or energy arrangement should now be underwritten assuming US administrative leverage can be invoked opportunistically, changing the required risk premium on such deals.
insights.quote: every lever that exists will get pulled regardless of the short and long-term consequences.

insights.claim: The Line 5 pipeline, which carries the majority of Ontario's imported oil (mostly Alberta crude transiting through the US Midwest), is Canada's single largest energy chokepoint: a shutdown would not cause an outright fuel shortage (Canada could partially compensate via rail and a reversed pipeline to Quebec with overseas oil backfill) but would substantially raise costs and could force the closure of one or more Ontario refineries that would lose cost-competitiveness against unaffected refiners.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: Ontario refining and downstream fuel-cost exposure to a Line 5 disruption is a live tail risk investors in Canadian energy/refining assets should model, even though outright supply failure is unlikely.
insights.quote: it would be not fatal but extremely ugly and ... in a single round prisoner's dilemma sense it'd be worth paying a fairly substantial cost to avoid that.

insights.claim: A proposed all-Canadian oil pipeline (Energy East or Northern Shield route, from Alberta through the Canadian Shield to Ontario and onward to Quebec/the Maritimes) would cost tens of billions of dollars and will never pencil out on pure economics, but is being evaluated as an insurance policy whose main value is that its mere existence removes the US's incentive to threaten Line 5, since cutting off a redundant supply route would just be self-defeating.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: Canadian pipeline nation-building projects should be evaluated as strategic-deterrence insurance rather than by standalone project economics, relevant to how governments and pension funds justify funding them.

insights.claim: Beyond Line 5, Canada's secondary energy vulnerabilities include eastern Canada's dependence on imported US natural gas (mitigated by underutilized/reactivatable pipeline capacity), a refining-capacity deficit in the Vancouver/lower mainland region (offset by Canada's counter-leverage as a crude exporter to US refiners), and Alberta's dependence on US diluent needed to thin bitumen for pipeline transport (offset because the US needs Alberta's bitumen for its own value-added refining).
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: These secondary vulnerabilities carry natural mutual counter-leverage that makes them less likely flashpoints than Line 5, helping investors rank the relative risk of different Canadian energy chokepoints.

insights.claim: A 'next tier' of Canadian vulnerability beyond physical energy infrastructure lies in financial services and IT: potential US sanctions on Canadian banks over US-dollar transactions, exclusion from the SWIFT system, or cutoffs of telecom/IT access to Europe or Asia -- prompting a stated preference for Canada to build mutual-defense arrangements with other 'middle powers' (e.g., France) that have similarly strong incentives not to abuse such leverage.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: Financial-sector and cross-border payments infrastructure should be viewed as a next-stage escalation risk in the trade war, relevant to Canadian banks' US-dollar clearing exposure and diversification planning.

themes.theme: Defense Procurement Sovereignty: F-35 vs. Gripen

insights.claim: The F-35 fighter jet uses a US-controlled parts-supply system (rather than buyer-held stockpiles) and US-managed mission-planning software that generates each flight's profile including sensitive data like air-defense and target locations, meaning the US could degrade or ground an ally's F-35 fleet within days to weeks by withholding parts or software access.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: Any NATO ally's F-35 fleet, including Canada's, carries a latent single-point-of-failure risk tied to US goodwill, a factor defense procurement and aerospace-supply-chain investors should weight alongside pure capability comparisons.
insights.quote: both of those are ... levers that if they were pulled would render the fleet either greatly degraded or inoperable in the space of days to weeks.

insights.claim: The Saab Gripen fighter uses a US-made engine but not a US-controlled parts system, and a buyer receives its own copy of the mission-planning software, allowing it to stockpile years of spare engine parts and manage its own updates -- making it a meaningfully lower-dependency alternative to the F-35 for a country like Canada seeking to reduce critical vulnerabilities to the US.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: Canada's fighter-jet procurement decision is framed as a strategic-sovereignty question, not just a cost/capability one, favoring a fleet mix that includes non-US-controlled platforms like the Gripen.

themes.theme: Nuclear Reactor Choice Recast as Geopolitical Risk

insights.claim: Westinghouse markets its AP-1000 reactor as '100% Canadian-owned' on Canadian podcasts but not on American ones, while it has become clear the US government treats Westinghouse as an instrument of American foreign policy (e.g., promoting Korean investment in the company); because the technology is US-domiciled, this creates real risk that US export restrictions could be applied to an AP-1000 project mid-construction or to its proprietary fuel/technical support.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: Ontario's multi-billion-dollar large-reactor decision between the AP-1000 and CANDU-based domestic technology should weight US export-control/geopolitical risk on the Westinghouse option, not just levelized cost -- directly relevant to Canadian nuclear-supply-chain and utility capex decisions.
insights.quote: it's becoming very clear that the US government regards Westinghouse as an instrument of American foreign policy.

insights.claim: The guest's own view on Canada's large-reactor choice shifted after witnessing the Gordie Howe Bridge episode -- now seeing CANDU and the Westinghouse AP-1000 as likely close enough in cost to warrant a genuinely competitive bid, with the deciding factor increasingly being whether Ontario should avoid creating a new critical dependency on a US-controlled reactor technology rather than which option pencils out cheapest.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: This signals a live shift in Canadian nuclear-industry and policy sentiment toward favoring domestic (CANDU) large-reactor technology on strategic-vulnerability grounds even absent a clear cost advantage, relevant to companies and suppliers positioned around either technology.
insights.quote: six months ago I may have had a somewhat different answer but ... The Gordy How Bridge was really my Joker moment on what kind of actions this admin or a future mega faction admin might have.

themes.theme: US Bond Market Fragility as a Two-Way Vulnerability

insights.claim: The United States runs a trade deficit nearly as large as Canada's entire GDP every year, a level considered unsustainable relative to its debt-to-GDP trajectory, and this deficit structurally depends on foreign central banks and investors continuing to recycle trade dollars into US Treasuries.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: The scale of the US trade deficit relative to Canada's GDP is a striking benchmark for gauging just how dependent US financing conditions are on continued foreign capital inflows -- a macro tail risk for rates and currency positioning.
insights.quote: the US has been running a trade deficit that's almost as big as the entire GDP of Canada every year.

insights.claim: If a broader trade war reduces global trade flows with the US, foreign central banks will naturally reduce their Treasury holdings to stay proportional to their (now smaller) trade relationship with the US, which reduces demand for Treasuries and pushes yields higher -- a dynamic already visible with US bond yields rising above 5% alongside tariff-driven inflation concerns.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: Investors should watch US Treasury yields as a direct market-based feedback channel through which an escalating trade war raises US government and consumer borrowing costs, independent of any deliberate retaliation.

insights.claim: Foreign central banks could apply a 'passive' form of financial retaliation against US tariff policy simply by not renewing (rolling over) maturing Treasuries one-for-one, or bank regulators could reduce the capital-reserve credit given to Treasuries (e.g., valuing them at 80-90% of face value instead of 100%), both of which would push US borrowing costs up sharply without any coordinated, explicit retaliatory action.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: This is a specific, plausible mechanism for a 'stealth' bond-market shock originating from trade-war fallout that fixed-income investors should monitor as a tail risk distinct from an overt sovereign-debt crisis.
insights.quote: a genie that pulled out of the bottle could not be put back in or at least not without another uh depression between now and then.

insights.claim: Rising inflation driven by tariffs -- not diplomacy or negotiation -- is identified as the most likely trigger that eventually forces the US to unwind Canada-specific tariffs, because reversing Canada tariffs is politically easy (a few executive orders and a 'bruised ego') compared to the much harder problem of reversing broad inflation once it takes hold.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: Investors looking for a resolution catalyst to the Canada-US trade war should watch US inflation and bond-yield data rather than diplomatic developments, since inflation crossing a political pain threshold is the more likely unwind trigger.
insights.quote: unwinding tariffs, especially with Canada, is just a couple of executive orders and a bruised ego where unwinding the inflation due to the ... Straits of Hormuz might be beyond ... mere mortals.

insights.claim: The historical Canada-US Auto Pact required only that as many cars be produced in Canada as sold in Canada -- not that they be the same models -- enabling specialization (e.g., a single plant building F-150s with 90% shipped to the US while nine other models were imported from the US) that created deep cross-border parts integration, such that no vehicle assembled in either country today is purely 'Canadian' or 'American.'
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: This history explains why unwinding US-Canada auto integration is far more disruptive than a simple tariff/reshoring narrative implies, since parts and sub-component supply chains -- not just final assembly -- are cross-border by design.

insights.claim: The Ambassador Bridge (Detroit-Windsor) historically carried roughly a billion dollars a day in trade flow, making it at one point the single highest-volume trade connection point in the world -- illustrating the scale of cross-border commerce (much of it automotive) now at risk in the trade war, though a new bridge (the Gordie Howe Bridge) will split those flows going forward.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: The sheer dollar volume through a single bridge crossing underscores the physical/logistics concentration risk in US-Canada trade that any serious decoupling strategy would need to address.
insights.quote: I think it was about a billion dollars a day if I remember the stats right.

insights.claim: China's EV manufacturing scale advantage is illustrated by BYD operating a single automotive factory with a footprint larger than the city of San Francisco, underscoring why preserving combined US-Canada auto market scale (rather than fragmenting it via tariffs) is viewed as strategically important for North American competitiveness against rising Chinese EV exports.
insights.speaker: Chris Keefer
insights.so_what: Auto-sector investors should weigh Chinese EV manufacturing scale (illustrated by BYD's giant single-site footprint) as the real competitive benchmark that US-Canada auto tariff disputes risk undermining rather than addressing.

insights.claim: If the US uses tariffs to try to collapse Canadian auto production and pull those jobs south, Canada's likely response is to redirect its own vehicle demand to 'anyone but American' imports, which would shrink total North American market scale rather than simply transfer jobs to the US as some administration factions assume -- undercutting the reshoring thesis's own logic.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: The 'main character syndrome' assumption that Canada will simply keep buying American cars if its own production is tariffed out of existence is likely wrong, a key risk for the reshoring thesis behind US auto tariffs.
insights.quote: the broad public mood now is very much in a anyone but American.

insights.claim: Despite pursuing reduced US dependency, Canada is not attempting full 'decoupling': roughly 70% of Canadian exports currently go to the US, and even with major investment in rail and port infrastructure to redirect trade toward Asia and Europe, that share might only fall to around 60%, showing a hard structural floor on how much Canada can realistically diversify away from the US market.
insights.speaker: Jesse Huebsch
insights.so_what: Canadian trade-diversification policy and any related infrastructure investment thesis (rail, ports) should be sized against a realistic 60-70% US export share, not a fantasy of full decoupling.
insights.quote: there's no decoupling from the United States 70% of our exports go to the US ... it may end up more like 60.
